#9899. Google claims last week’s critical VMware bug was under attack in September

China-linked ARMORY CASTLE knew about it weeks before it unleashed five custom malware tools targeting vCenter

Google’s Mandiant unit has claimed that the critical flaw VMware last week revealed in its vCenter product was under attack by a China-linked threat actor which knew of the bug in July and exploited it in September.

VMware revealed several flaws on November 19. The big nasty is CVE-2026-123890, which allows unauthorized access to vCenter, the management console for hosts and guest VMs.

According to seven researchers from Google’s threat intelligence group (formerly Mandiant), a crew it calls ARMORY CASTLE that it suspects of having links to the People’s Republic of China exploited CVE-2026-123890 by first compromising remote access appliances from BeyondTrust.

Google’s analysis suggests the crew uses that toehold to establish access to other Linux appliances before moving deeper into victims’ networks.

If the crew finds vCenter, it deploys a custom malware tool called “BONESAW” designed to slice into the VMware product. In the incident Google observed, BONESAW let attackers “forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user.”

The gang put that access to work by conducting an inventory of the victim’s VMware setup, scooping up data describing the ESXi file system, attached disks, and mounted Virtual Machine File System volumes. ARMORY CASTLE also added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys, and “conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account.”

Google also found evidence of BONESAW being used in July, on a server an unidentified entity had patched against CVE-2026-59309 – another authentication bypass vulnerability in vCenter.

And BONESAW was just one of five tools Google thinks ARMORY CASTLE created as part of its plan to attack vCenter. It also made webshells named SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, a backdoor called BEARBONES, and a SAML utility called SAWSNAKE.

“The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations,” Google’s researchers wrote. “It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets.”

Few targets are as juicy as vCenter, because it can literally give attackers access to thousands of virtual machines and the hosts they run on.

Google hasn't said how many attacks is saw on vCenter using BONESAW.

The Register asked VMware if it was aware of the September attack, if it took any measures to defend its customers at the time, and to share a timeline for disclosure and remediation of CVE-2026-123890.

A spokesperson responded by pointing to VMware’s Q&A document and stating “In today's threat environment, customers should assume any publicly disclosed critical vulnerability can and will be exploited by threat actors under the right conditions and should apply the recommended patches immediately.”

VMware has tried to make that easier by adding non-disruptive patching to several of its products, and introducing a product called vDefend that offers “virtual patching” by creating compensating controls that use network micro segmentation and other techniques to block access to resources malware uses. Last month, VMware debuted another new tool, HyperArmor, to block incoming malicious traffic targeting its VCF private cloud suite.

In recent discussions with The Register, VMware execs told us the Broadcom business unit will emphasize security improvements in future product releases.

“Our teams have integrated frontier AI security model testing directly into our engineering workflows, strengthened our software supply chain to reduce third-party dependencies and speed up upstream responses, and built VCF 9.1 specifically for high-velocity security,” a spokesperson said in response to questions about the Mandiant report.

One security offering VMware won’t continue is free access to patches for zero-day flaws in supported versions of products sold under its old perpetual licenses – even to users who don’t have an ongoing support deal or software subscription.

VMware last year stopped making those patches available for download and promised it would establish “a separate patch delivery cycle.”

Readers have pointed out that information about the new cycle isn’t easy to find, and The Register noticed that the blog post in which Broadcom CEO Hock Tan promised the free patches no longer contains references to the offer. Removing the promise seems to be a recent edit as an Internet Archive snapshot of the page from October 20 does mention the zero-day patch freebies.

A VMware spokesperson told us the free zero-day patch policy remains in place despite changes to the post.

“Broadcom’s policy to provide access to zero-day critical security patches to customers who, at their own risk, continue to run perpetual VMware vSphere 8 software without an active support agreement, remains in place,” the spokesperson wrote. “Those customers can get these patches by contacting Broadcom. This policy covers vSphere 8 patches only and is expected to remain in effect through the end of general support on October 11, 2027.” ®

With the flick of a switch, he smoked out competent PC maintenance skills

#9898. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with new runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

From there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the new one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and shows exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three important properties:

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:

Or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:

funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent says so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

Published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious

Your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

#9897. GhostScript CVE 2026-125396: "Upload2Shell"

Paulos Yibelo · pwn.ai · 21 November 2026

Our previous research into ImageMagick's format handling and security policies showed how files with trusted extensions such as .jpg and .png could be handed to an unexpected interpreter. In this article, we show how we reached Ghostscript through most of the applications we tested, exploited a memory corruption bug in its font loader, and bypassed its -dSAFER sandbox to achieve remote command execution across widely used software.

On 25 September, we posted a short announcement naming some of the applications and services our research had reached. The list came from following file-processing dependencies across products that otherwise had little in common.

That gave us two connected questions to investigate: which interpreters could we reach through ordinary application features, and could those interpreters safely process the files we sent? We continued into Ghostscript's internals and found several independent bugs of varying impact. We reported them to Artifex and worked with affected platforms to harden their file processing. Some of those bugs are still being fixed.

This article follows one of the more interesting findings. Upload2Shell, now CVE-2026-125396, is a use-after-free in Ghostscript's Type 1 font loader. It gave us a write-what-where primitive: the ability to choose both the data written and its destination in native memory. A crafted document could use that control to alter the state enforcing -dSAFER and run commands as the rendering process.

Almost every application we tested with file uploads could be tricked into passing a file with a trusted extension to Ghostscript. A feature as routine as cropping an image or generating a preview could expose the interpreter. With the primitive working, we followed those conversion paths back out to their remote entry points.

Consider a PHP application generating a preview. Its code calls Imagick, the PHP binding to ImageMagick. ImageMagick selects a format handler, which may delegate the rendering to Ghostscript or another interpreter. The upload endpoint does not have to start gs itself; it only has to pass the file to a library that will.

Our WordPress-shaped preview proof reached that delegate through Imagick::readImage($input . '[0]'). The filename ended in .pdf, but the bytes were PostScript; ImageMagick handed them to Ghostscript under -dSAFER. The exploit also needed a Type 1 font file. In this delegate, it wrote the font to the scratch output path already authorized in currentpagedevice /OutputFile; another self-contained variant used Ghostscript's process-local %ram% device. Neither needed a pre-existing font file on the server.

Ghostscript can also be linked into an image-processing build as a library. In that arrangement, the interpreter runs inside the existing process instead of appearing as a separate gs command. Looking only for explicit Ghostscript calls in application code misses both kinds of indirect invocation.

An application does not need to call gs itself. In our separate decoder tests, the following ordinary image calls reached Ghostscript when given EPS content, even when the file was named .png.

Image.open() alone only identified the file in our test. Loading pixels, cropping, or converting them started the renderer.

Our source audit also found image decoding calls in InvokeAI uploads, AUTOMATIC1111 img2img, and ComfyUI previews.

We tested the calls developers use after accepting an image. Across two controlled runs on Ubuntu 24.04 with Ghostscript installed, one matrix traced 145 benign calls across 29 image APIs and the other covered additional wrappers including Imagick and imageio. We also gave the PostScript sample a .png name. It was not a valid PNG; this tested whether the decoder trusted the name or inspected the bytes. The versions below describe the tested libraries, not every product that uses them.

The decoder matters. PHP GD, OpenCV, prebuilt Sharp, Jimp, Java ImageIO, and Go's standard image decoders did not start Ghostscript for these inputs. Copying or storing a file did not render it either; the later preview or conversion is the step to inspect.

Ghostscript renders both PDF and PostScript. PostScript is a Turing-complete programming language used to describe pages, so rendering a PostScript document means executing a program. Ghostscript's -dSAFER sandbox restricts that program's file access and command execution. Like seccomp, it limits what untrusted code can do, but the enforcement is different: -dSAFER relies on checks inside the interpreter rather than a kernel-enforced system-call filter.

That still leaves a large interpreter exposed to attacker-controlled programs. As with a JavaScript engine such as V8, running the language is expected; a memory-safety bug can let a program corrupt the engine running it. An attacker can develop and test that program as a PostScript file, then deliver it through an ordinary upload.

Those permission checks matter because the rendering process has access of its own. Its service account may be able to read application files, write to disk, and start other programs. The sandbox is supposed to keep an untrusted document from using that authority. Loading a font is one of the ordinary rendering operations that must respect this boundary.

GPT 5.6 Sol, working with @PaulosYibelo, found the issue in .putgstringcopy, a helper in Resource/Init/gs_fonts.ps. Ghostscript implements parts of its own font loading in PostScript. This helper needed to write into protected font dictionaries, so it used an internal operation called .forceput.

Ordinary document code should not have that ability. The helper was bound and marked executeonly, protecting its implementation from direct inspection. But it still had to execute, and one of the operations before its privileged write could fail. The relevant sequence was:

The first line copies a string. The second performs the protected store and restores the allocation mode. The helper did not first check that its operands were of the expected types.

We registered a Type 1 font in Fontmap and loaded it with findfont. The font defined an ordinary Courier-derived face, but its loading code could see the font loader's operand stack. It replaced the filename string on that stack with a local array. In the global-to-local conversion branch, length and string allocation succeeded; copy then raised typecheck because its source was an array.

The document's error handler returned with the stack prepared for the next operation in the already-bound helper. This is the operative excerpt from our proof:

The five pops discard the failing copy, its new destination string, our substituted filename, the loader's /PathLoad key, and the loaded font dictionary. They leave the saved allocation-mode boolean on the stack. Our chosen dictionary, key, and value follow it. Execution resumes at .forceput; the subsequent setglobal consumes the boolean. We never had to call the hidden operator directly.

One implementation detail made that recovered write more than a protected-dictionary edit. In psi/zgeneric.c, .forceput temporarily treats systemdict as local while it stores the value, then restores the dictionary's space flags. A local object can therefore pass the store check into a dictionary that survives a later restore.

A protected dictionary write alone does not explain native code execution. The next step broke a separate rule: a reference must not remain usable after its object has been reclaimed.

PostScript distinguishes local and global virtual memory. Here, “virtual memory” refers to the interpreter's object spaces. A save records local memory state; a later restore discards objects created since that save. Global objects can survive that restoration.

That creates a lifetime constraint. A surviving global dictionary must not keep a usable reference to a local object that restore will free. Otherwise, restoring the local space leaves the dictionary pointing into reclaimed storage.

Our recovered store let us create precisely that relationship:

The reference in the dictionary had not changed. What occupied the address had.

A small probe made the reuse visible before we touched native memory. This excerpt omits the font setup and error handler; findfont triggers the recovered .forceput, which places a local array in systemdict:

The last read comes from Replacement; the write goes through the stale systemdict reference. If the freed allocation is reused, Replacement[1] reads 5151. The two references have reached the same bytes.

The native proof uses the same idea with a dangling 2,048-byte string and fresh arrays of integers. Each integer is 0x12345678. We scan the stale string for the marker's bytes, change its low byte from 0x78 to 0x79, then find the live array element that became 0x12345679. That identifies the overlapping slot; no absolute heap address has to be guessed.

On our 64-bit build, a Ghostscript ref occupies 16 bytes: eight bytes for its type, attributes, and size, followed by eight bytes for its value or pointer. We saved a valid integer ref for cleanup and the header of a valid writable string ref as a template. Then we placed currentdevice in the overlapping array slot, read its genuine device-reference pointer through the dangling string, and changed the live ref into a temporary string view over that pointer. The byte view let us follow Ghostscript's own pointers:

Those structure offsets describe the tested x86-64 build; the address of each object came from a live interpreter reference. This is why the proof did not depend on a fixed process address. We restored the forged ref to its original integer form before exercising file or command access.

We demonstrated native control in production image and document pipelines with a reversible change to an arithmetic operator. We copied the 16-byte mul reference, obtained a genuine sub reference, and replaced only the eight pointer bytes at offset 8 in the live mul ref. We invoked that same ref once and copied the original 16 bytes back. This was a C function-pointer change, not a PostScript definition of a new mul.

The returned page recorded the before, during, and after values:

The middle result is 29 - 11. The captured proof output also recorded NATIVE_POINTER_OVERWRITE_MATCHED=true and NATIVE_DISPATCH_RESTORED=true. For most reports, we used a simpler proof that read /proc/version and returned its contents. The arithmetic test demonstrated native control; the file read demonstrated that we had crossed Ghostscript's file-access boundary.

The same byte view gave us a target for command execution: Ghostscript's native path-control state. After walking the pointer chain above, Target was the forged string view over gs_lib_ctx_core_t. The decisive write in the proof was four PostScript put operations on native bytes:

Those bytes were path_control_active. The proof read 1,0,0,0 before the write and 0,0,0,0 after it, then confirmed that .currentpathcontrolstate was false. -dSAFER was still on the Ghostscript command line; its native file-path check had been disabled in memory.

That was not the only check. The proof first used the recovered .forceput to set the PostScript-side PermitFileWriting list to [ (*) ]. For %pipe%, parse_file_name() also consulted a cached LockFilePermissions flag. We loaded the font a third time, force-wrote that protected user parameter to false, and used save/restore to synchronize the cached value. The recorded sequence makes the separate gates visible:

The bounded Debian print job ended with this command proof, writing only a marker in /var/tmp:

The scheduler recorded PIPE_RCE_STOPPED=false, and the marker file appeared on the print server. false here means the stopped block completed. The command ran as uid=7(lp), the renderer's account, not as the person who submitted the job.

With the interpreter primitive established, the next question was where a remote user could supply the document. We traced how popular applications invoked image and PDF processing. Three cases show how different the entry points could be.

An attacker only had to send a crafted email to someone using the Roundcube server and have the recipient view the message. The sender needed no Roundcube account. The recipient did not have to click or download the attachment: displaying the email triggered the server-side processing that ran our command.

Our attachment was declared as image/jpeg and named quarterly-results.jpg, but its contents were PostScript. Roundcube treated it as an image and automatically requested a thumbnail. The thumbnail path passed the attachment to ImageMagick, which invoked Ghostscript. The document ran our proof command as www-data and produced a thumbnail.

We reached the same Ghostscript interpreter while WordPress generated a preview for an uploaded PDF. In WordPress Core, media upload privileges were enough: Authors and higher roles have them by default. Plugins using WordPress's upload and preview functions exposed the same path. WordPress's CVE-2026-65640 advisory describes remote code execution on sites using Imagick and Ghostscript. On our Linux systems, that was the stack handling the uploads.

Plugins exposed that processing to visitors without an account. In Forminator, we used a public PDF field configured to store the upload in the Media Library. That caused WordPress to generate attachment metadata and enter the Imagick conversion path. Essential Addons for Elementor's public registration widget provided another route through its upload field. Both chains ran the command as the web-service user. Once the file reached the renderer, the font-loader flaw was the same.

We also reached Ghostscript through CUPS on Debian 13 and other Linux distributions. On Debian 13, we sent an IPP Print-Job to a shared network queue that accepted jobs without authentication. CUPS passed our PostScript document to gstopdf, which started the distribution's Ghostscript with -dSAFER. The command ran on the print server as uid=7(lp).

Our RCE proof executed one fixed command and wrote a marker under /var/tmp. Requiring authentication on the queue blocked the unauthenticated submission. Shared queues that accept network print jobs without credentials expose the renderer to anyone who can reach them.

The Ghostscript CVE scores the interpreter flaw at 8.5 under CVSS 4.0. That rating uses a local attack vector. Our demonstrations reached the interpreter remotely, through both production services and the applications described here. CUPS supplied a network-exploitable print path; Roundcube supplied an email-based remote exploit; WordPress and its plugins supplied remotely exploitable upload paths. The recorded trials show that these chains were repeatable. The attacker could deliver the exploit remotely, despite the interpreter's local attack-vector classification.

The first ten rows show Upload2Shell proofs in products or their shipped components. The rows after them trace more upload and preview paths. Each entry gives the access, tested stack or pinned source revision, and the processing step that matters.

Our Ghostscript research also reached Google, Dropbox, and other production services whose names are redacted. The table brings those production services together; the Dropbox and redacted findings have separate roots from the Type 1 bug described in this article.

The renderer's account and the surrounding system controls determine what follows native memory control. That is why the table records process privileges and the observed result alongside the application name.

Here is a complete, self-contained PostScript proof of the native operator write described above. It writes its Type 1 font to Ghostscript's process-local %ram% device, triggers the font-loader flaw, reuses the freed allocation, changes a live mul reference to call sub, and restores the original bytes. No companion font file is needed.

Each step below points to its lines in the full file. The 29 × 11 check returns 319 before and after the write. While the pointer is changed, it returns 18, the result of subtraction. This proof demonstrates native memory control; the command-execution chain described above changes Ghostscript's path-control state instead.

The file changes native memory inside the rendering process. It does not execute a shell command or touch host files. On the fixed 10.08.0 build, the dangling-reference lookup failed before the pointer write.

Artifex's first fix checks the operands before .putgstringcopy can fail in copy. That closes the error path we used to recover the privileged store. A subsequent change moves the helper into C and removes its dependence on .forceput.

The first patch also explains why this kind of operation has been difficult to remove. Artifex was already working to eliminate or minimize its use. As the maintainer put it:

“it isn't easy to undo 30 years worth of assumptions in the code.” Ken Sharp, Artifex, in the fix for bug 709684

An internal font loader needed a write that ordinary document code could not perform. An error exposed that authority to the document, and the document used it to violate an object-lifetime rule. The final memory corruption depended on assumptions made at several different layers.

The applications had their own opportunities to interrupt the chain. WordPress released its Core mitigation in 7.0.4 on 12 August, with backports to older supported branches. Its application CVE and the Ghostscript CVE address different points in the processing path. For the CUPS route, queue authentication controls who can submit the document. A policy that prevents a renderer from starting a shell can limit what happens even after the interpreter is compromised.

The fix has to reach the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript inside an existing container image or application bundle. A document worker can therefore keep using vulnerable code after the host's package has been replaced.

Application hardening can close a route into the interpreter as well. The Roundcube sequence illustrates why the order of operations matters: checking a file's real type after generating its thumbnail gives the renderer the first chance to interpret it. For each downstream service, the useful question is what changed in the path from the submitted file to the rendering process.

Artifex released the root fix in Ghostscript 10.08.0 on 8 September 2026. Many distributions have since shipped it, either in that release or as a backport to an older version. Ubuntu published fixes for seven releases; Debian patched Trixie and its development branches.

The coverage is uneven. As of 12 November, Debian still listed Bookworm as vulnerable, Amazon Linux listed a pending fix, and several SUSE branches remained affected or in progress. Applications on those branches can still expose the flaw when their file-processing path reaches the affected Ghostscript package. A distribution name or a recent update to another Ghostscript CVE is not enough to establish that this bug is fixed.

The tables below record the package status for this specific flaw. Older version numbers can include a backported fix; a published fixed version does not establish that every application or container has adopted it.

As of 12 November 2026, the following vendor trackers still listed a vulnerable, affected, or pending Ghostscript package for this exact flaw. These labels describe package status, not a tested remote application path. Check the package actually installed or bundled by each service.

We did not establish whether current RHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages contain the .putgstringcopy fix.

Ubuntu's USN-8949-1, published on 21 October 2026, describes our font-operand finding and lists fixed Ghostscript packages for seven releases. The notice predates the CVE assignment, so it labels this finding “No CVE number.” These are package fixes, not additional remote application tests.

Debian's tracker records the first fixed source version for Trixie and unstable. The testing branch later received the upstream-fixed package. Debian 12 remains listed vulnerable in the vendor-status table above.

The records below show packages containing upstream Ghostscript 10.08.0 or an advisory-listed fixed build. A package appearing here does not establish the first fixed date for every architecture or branch.

Fixed Ghostscript builds also reached Windows and macOS packaging channels. The availability of a package does not tell us which Ghostscript binary a particular application uses.

The dependency problem is easy to miss from the top of an application. Several layers below, a file may enter PostScript or another interpreter that never appeared in the application's security review. A review that checks only whether the upload handler accepts trusted file types can miss a vulnerability in the code that eventually processes them. A penetration test that stops at the same boundary has the same blind spot.

Alongside this Type 1 issue, our broader Ghostscript audit reached production services at Dropbox and other redacted vendors through separate findings. Each program paid its maximum bounty. Their case studies will explain the individual root causes and proofs once we have permission to publish the technical details. The series is organized around the underlying bugs as well as the products.

WordPress released its mitigation on 12 August. Artifex authored the Ghostscript fix on 2 September, committed it on 7 September, and released 10.08.0 on 8 September. We completed the Debian network CUPS proof on 17 September. The Ghostscript CVE was published on 9 November in US Eastern time.

The Debian 13 CUPS chain will be the first full case study and PoC in this series. The other product writeups will follow, with the build, delivery path, exploit result, and vendor response for each. We will add their links to the tables as they appear.

We expect other researchers to find more applications affected by this flaw. The useful place to look is the processing that follows an accepted file: thumbnail generation, metadata extraction, document import, and print conversion. Each can hand an attacker-controlled document to a process with access the sender does not have. Upload2Shell let the document use that access for itself.

#9896. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. #9894. Probabilistic data structures in Go, part 2

Probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle. Does the set contain a certain item? How many unique items are in the collection? What is the 99th percentile in a stream of numbers? How similar are two sets? Unlike deterministic structures, the answers might not be exact, but in return, you can save a lot of memory.

Previously, we reviewed the following data structures: Bloom filter (for checking if an item is in a set), Count-min sketch (for counting items), HyperLogLog (for counting unique items), T-digest (for finding quantiles), and Top-k (for finding the most frequent items).

In this post, we'll talk about other probabilistic structures and compare them to the ones we've already covered. We'll look at how they work and what kinds of guarantees they provide.

All examples use unsure — a package that implements these structures in Go.

Binary fuse filter • UltraLogLog • Log-linear histogram • MinHash

A binary fuse filter is a set that trades certainty for space, like a Bloom filter1. It can tell you that an item is definitely not in the set, or that it probably is (which might be a false positive). The filter doesn't store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

Unlike a Bloom filter, a binary fuse filter is static: you build it once from all the items, and you can't add more later. In exchange, it uses less memory than a Bloom filter with the same false positive rate. For example, a fuse filter for 1,000,000 items with a 0.39% false positive rate takes 1.13 MB (9 bits per item), while a Bloom filter takes 1.51 MB (12 bits per item).

This makes binary fuse filters a good fit for data that is written once and read many times, like the key set of an immutable file in a database (to skip files that don't have the key), or a list of known bad items, such as leaked passwords or malicious URLs.

The fingerprint type (T in New[T]) determines the false positive rate and the memory use:

The constructor takes an iterator of items to add to the filter and the expected number of items (0 if unknown). The number is only used to preallocate memory, so a good estimate makes the build faster.

You can check if an item is in the filter, but you cannot add or delete an item, count the number of items, or iterate over them.

The filter2 is an array of b-bit fingerprints (for example, b = 8 for uint8). Each item is hashed to a 64-bit value h, which gives the item's fingerprint f (b bits computed from h) and three positions in the array (cells). The array is filled so that for every item, the XOR of its cells equals f.

To check an item, you compute h, look up its three cells, and compare their XOR with f. For an item in the set, they always match. For any other item, the XOR is a random b-bit value, which matches f with probability 2^-b.

Each check reads three cells, so for large filters it's three cache misses, against one for a blocked Bloom filter. However, since the reads are independent, the CPU can do them concurrently, so the checks are about as fast as with a Bloom filter.

The filter uses the local wyhash3 implementation for hashing. It performs roughly the same as xxh34 but has a much simpler implementation, without SIMD or assembly.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks5, comparing unsure to xorfilter6 (binary fuse by the authors of the paper) and bloom (unsure's own Bloom filter) with 8-bit fingerprints (ns/op, lower is better):

Unsure is the same size as xorfilter (same layout) with up to 25% faster checks. Compared to the Bloom filter, it uses up to 36% less memory, with checks as fast or faster, but up to 2.5× slower builds.

Bloom filter overview and how it works. ↩︎

Binary Fuse Filters paper by Thomas Mueller Graf and Daniel Lemire, 2022. ↩︎

Reference wyhash implementation by Wang Yi. ↩︎

Reference xxHash implementation by Yann Collet. ↩︎

FastFilter/xorfilter by Daniel Lemire. ↩︎

UltraLogLog is a unique items counter that trades accuracy for space, like HyperLogLog7. It tells you approximately how many distinct items it has seen, no matter how many times each one appeared. UltraLogLog doesn't store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

UltraLogLog is a newer design (Otmar Ertl, 2024) that uses the space more efficiently: for the same error, it needs about 43% less memory than HyperLogLog. For example, a HyperLogLog sketch with 0.81% standard error takes 16 KB, while an UltraLogLog sketch with 0.86% error takes 8 KB. However, adding, counting, and merging are slower than with HyperLogLog.

UltraLogLog is useful in the same places as HyperLogLog: counting unique visitors, unique search queries, or distinct values in a database column, possibly across many machines or segments.

You can merge sketches to get the total number of unique items from all of them, without counting shared items twice.

The sketch has one setting: the precision p, which gives a relative standard error of 0.782/√(2^p). The default is p=13 with 0.86% error in 8 KB, close to the common HyperLogLog default (0.81% in 16 KB).

You can add items to a sketch, get the estimated count, and merge sketches. You cannot check if a specific item was added, remove items, or list them.

HyperLogLog hashes each item and uses the first p bits of the hash to pick one of m = 2^p registers. It calculates the rank (the number of leading zeros in the rest of the hash, plus one) and keeps the highest rank it has seen in the register. Seeing a rank of k suggests there were about 2^k items in the register. The count is estimated from all the registers together.

A HyperLogLog register loses some information: it only keeps track of the highest value, not whether any slightly lower values were seen. These lower values show up at least as often as the highest one, so they can tell a lot about the count.

UltraLogLog8 uses the registers more efficiently. Each register is still one byte, but it stores the highest rank k in the upper 6 bits, and whether k−1 and k−2 were seen in the lower 2 bits:

The count estimate uses the FGRA estimator from the UltraLogLog paper. Each register adds a weight based on its value, and the count is calculated as a power of the sum of the weights. Nearly empty and nearly full sketches get special handling, so the estimate stays accurate from zero to billions of items, without bias tables or a separate formula for small counts.

Unsure keeps a histogram of register values (256 four-byte counters, 1 KB) updated as the registers change. This way, Count reads the histogram instead of scanning all the registers. Merge checks 8 registers at a time using a few bitwise operations to find which ones the other sketch would change, and only updates those.

The item is hashed once with wyhash, and the 64-bit hash is split into the register index and the rank.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks9, comparing UltraLogLog to unsure's own HyperLogLog and axiom10 (HyperLogLog with LogLog-Beta estimator and sparse mode) (ns/op, lower is better):

Accuracy and memory, relative RMSE over 1,000 sketches (lower is better):

UltraLogLog provides the same accuracy as HyperLogLog with almost half the memory. However, adding, counting, and merging are noticeably slower.

HyperLogLog overview and how it works. ↩︎

UltraLogLog paper by Otmar Ertl, 2024. ↩︎

A log-linear histogram is a summary of a stream of numbers that trades accuracy for space. It can give you an approximate median, 99th percentile, or any other quantile of the data. It can also estimate what fraction of the numbers are below a certain value (the CDF). The histogram doesn't store the numbers, so it's much more compact than a sorted list.

For example, to find the exact 99th percentile of 1,000,000 response times, you'd have to keep all of them. With 64-bit floats, that takes 8 MB. A log-linear histogram estimates the same percentile within 0.39% of its true value using about 14 KB — almost 600 times less.

The error is relative to the value: if the true 99th percentile is 200 ms, the histogram returns a value between 199.2 and 200.8 ms. This guarantee applies to every quantile, from the median to the most extreme outliers. The size of the histogram doesn't depend on the number of values, only on the accuracy you choose and on how wide the range of the values is.

A log-linear histogram is useful when you need percentiles for positive values that cover a wide range, like latencies, file sizes, or prices.

You can merge histograms to gather data from multiple machines or segments (like by hour, endpoint, or region). Merging is exact: a merged histogram is the same as if it had received all the values directly.

The histogram has two settings: relative error and value range. By default, the error is 0.0039 (0.39%) and the range is from 1e-9 to 1e18. Lowering the error or increasing the range uses more memory.

You can add numbers to a histogram, estimate quantiles and the CDF, and merge histograms. You cannot remove numbers or list them.

A histogram splits the range of values into buckets and counts how many values are in each one. To estimate a quantile, it adds up the counts starting from the lowest bucket until it reaches the requested rank, then returns a value from that bucket. The accuracy of the estimate depends on how wide the bucket is.

With buckets that have equal widths, like 0–10, 10–20, and so on, every estimate has the same absolute error of ±5 around the bucket's midpoint. So the relative error is very large for small values and unnecessarily small for large values:

A logarithmic histogram solves this by making each bucket's width proportional to its value. For example, if the bucket boundaries are powers of 1.02 (1, 1.02, 1.0404, ...), the end of each bucket is 2% larger than its start, so any value in the bucket is within about 1% of the bucket's midpoint. DDSketch11 uses this method. The downside is that finding the right bucket for a value means you have to calculate a logarithm, which is relatively slow.

A log-linear histogram gets almost the same result with cheaper math. First, it splits the values into ranges between powers of two: 1–2, 2–4, 4–8, and so on (these are called octaves). Then it splits every octave into the same number of equal-width buckets. For example, here are three octaves with 4 buckets each:

Each octave is twice as long as the previous one, so its buckets are twice as wide, and the bucket width grows with the values, as in a logarithmic histogram. Finding the right bucket only takes a few bit operations instead of calculating a logarithm.

HdrHistogram12 is the best-known log-linear histogram. It records integers: the position of the highest 1 bit of a number determines its octave, and the next few bits determine the bucket within the octave.

Unsure works with float64 numbers and finds the bucket in a similar way to HdrHistogram.

A float64 in Go (and most other languages) is made up of three parts:

The number's value is 1.f × 2^e, where 1.f is a binary fraction between 1 and 2.

The exponent determines the octave, from 2^e to 2^(e+1). The top m bits of the mantissa determine one of the 2^m equal buckets within the octave.

For example, here's the number 5.25 with m=3 (8 buckets per octave). In binary, 5.25 = 1.0101₂ × 2², so the exponent is 2 (stored as 1025), and the mantissa starts with 0101:

Add finds the bucket for the given number and increases the count. Merge adds the counts bucket by bucket. Quantile adds up the counts from the closer end (the leftmost bucket for q ≤ 0.5, the rightmost bucket otherwise) until it reaches the rank.

The number of mantissa bits m comes from the requested error: the constructor picks the smallest m for which the maximum error doesn't exceed the requested one. The default is m=7: 128 buckets per octave and an error of 0.39%.

A t-digest13 also estimates quantiles, but it limits the error in ranks: Quantile(0.99) returns a value whose rank is close to 99%. A log-linear histogram limits the error in values: Quantile(0.99) returns a value close to the true 99th percentile.

In the middle of the data, the two are pretty similar. But in a long tail, values at nearby ranks can be very different, so even a small error in rank can lead to a big difference in value. Here is the mean relative error of an 8.5 KB t-digest (δ=100) on 1M values from three distributions: lognormal (as in the benchmarks), Pareto with α=1.5 (a longer tail), and uniform between 1,000,000 and 2,000,000 (no tail):

A log-linear histogram of about the same size (1% error, 8 KB) has an error below 0.78% for all these cases.

So a log-linear histogram is better for latencies, sizes, and other positive measurements with long tails. A t-digest is better when you need a fixed size no matter what the values are, or when the values can be arbitrarily close to zero.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks14, comparing unsure to hdr15 (log-linear, integers only, fixed range) and dd16 (DDSketch, logarithmic buckets) with a lognormal distribution (ns/op, lower is better):

Mean relative error at the requested 0.1%, over 1M values (lower is better):

Memory after adding 1M values (lower is better):

Unsure adds values as fast as hdr and 5× faster than dd, queries 5–19× faster than hdr and about 35× faster than dd, and merges about as fast as dd and 35–175× faster than hdr. It's slightly less accurate than hdr (using 5× less memory), and more accurate than dd (using 1.4× more memory).

DDSketch paper by Charles Masson et al., 2019. ↩︎

HdrHistogram/hdrhistogram-go by Coda Hale. ↩︎

MinHash estimates how similar two sets are. It summarizes each set in a short fixed-size signature (for example, 256 numbers). Comparing two signatures gives the approximate Jaccard similarity of the sets: |A∩B| / |A∪B|, the proportion of unique items that both sets share.

The size of a signature doesn't depend on the size of the set, so you can compare two sets of a million items each just by comparing 256 pairs of numbers instead of checking every item. Plus, each set's signature is only calculated once, so comparing lots of sets to each other is relatively cheap.

MinHash is useful for finding near-duplicate documents, like web pages or essays (represented as sets of words or 3-word phrases). It's also useful for finding similar user profiles (as sets of liked items) or overlapping datasets (as sets of keys).

The MinHash sketch has one setting: the signature size k, which gives a standard error of √(J(1−J)/k) for true similarity J. For example, with k=256 and J=0.5:

You can add items to a sketch, merge sketches, and get and compare signatures. You cannot check if a specific item was added, count the items, remove them, or list them.

Classic MinHash17 hashes every item with k different hash functions. Here are two sets, A = {fox, cat, dog, owl} and B = {fox, dog, emu}, and their item hashes for k=4:

For each hash function, the set keeps only the smallest hash value among its items. These k minimums are the set's signature. To estimate the similarity of two sets, compare their signatures position by position, count the number of equal values, and divide by k:

The estimated similarity (0.5) is different from the actual value (2 shared items / 5 distinct items = 0.4). To get a more accurate estimate, k is usually much larger than in this example.

One permutation hashing18 hashes every item once, with a single hash function, and splits the range of hash values into k equal buckets. Each bucket keeps the smallest hash value among its items. Here are the same sets with k=4, using h1 from above:

Each bucket works like a separate MinHash over the items in its range. So the bucket minimums form a signature, and comparing two signatures works the same way. But there is a catch: when a set isn't much larger than k, some buckets end up empty (shown as · above), so there's nothing to compare in them.

Optimal densification19 solves this by filling each empty bucket with the value from another bucket in the same set. Each empty bucket tries other buckets in a pseudo-random order and copies the value of the first non-empty one:

This order depends only on the empty bucket's position, so two similar sets tend to fill empty spots with the same values. This makes the estimate work for sets of any size, with about the same error as classic MinHash.

Unsure keeps the k bucket minimums in the sketch. Add and Merge use the original buckets. Densification only happens in Signature, and it makes a copy of the buckets without modifying the sketch.

Each item is hashed once with 64-bit wyhash. Multiplying the hash by k once gives both the bucket and the value to store:

Densification fills empty buckets in a coordinated way, spreading the copies evenly across the non-empty buckets. This keeps the error close to classic MinHash, and makes densification fast even for small sets.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks20, comparing unsure to dgryski21 (classic MinHash) (ns/op, lower is better):

RMSE of the similarity estimate at k=256 and J=0.5 (lower is better):

Unsure adds items 6–70× faster than dgryski, compares signatures at the same speed, has roughly the same accuracy, and uses half the memory.

Classic MinHash paper by Andrei Broder, 1997. ↩︎

One permutation hashing by Ping Li et al., 2012. ↩︎

Optimal densification paper by Anshumali Shrivastava, 2017. ↩︎

Bloom filter and HyperLogLog are everyone's favorites, but they're not the only useful probabilistic data structures out there. In some situations, you might find these helpful:

To use them in Go, try the nalgeon/unsure package:

InfoQ Homepage News Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency below 1 MS

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read

Uber has redesigned its Go-based translation cache to reduce its initial memory footprint by more than 90% while keeping p99 cache miss latency below one millisecond. The hybrid architecture retains translation keys and frequently accessed values in memory while storing the remaining values on disk. The system serves millions of translations per second and maintains a cache hit rate above 99.9%.

The optimization addresses two problems identified through memory profiling across Uber's Go services. Garbage collection (GC) consumed more than 20% of CPU utilization in some services, with translations accounting for approximately 70% of allocated objects.

At Uber's scale, even small inefficiencies in memory management can add up.

The first optimization replaced Go's sync.Map with a conventional map[string]string protected by an RWMutex. The workload was predominantly read-heavy, with infrequent updates and no individual deletions. The previous implementation created multiple objects and pointers for each translation entry, increasing GC overhead. Moving to a value-based map reduced object allocations and improved CPU utilization by more than 30% in the affected service.

However, reducing object allocations did not solve the overall memory consumption problem. Translation datasets could contain two to three million keys, although individual services typically accessed only a small subset. Cache refreshes introduced another issue: the service built a replacement cache in the background before atomically swapping it with the existing one. Both copies therefore occupied memory simultaneously, causing some services to run out of memory during refreshes.

Uber considered external caching and generating service-specific translation subsets, but both introduced additional operational or maintenance costs. The team instead adopted a hybrid storage design that preserves the existing Get() and Put() API. All keys remain available in memory for fast lookups, while translation values are stored in disk-backed files.

Uber's hybrid translation cache (Source: Uber Blog Post)

The implementation uses 256 shards, each with its own read-write mutex, in-memory entries, and disk file. Six-byte hash-based keys reduce metadata overhead, with a fallback to the original key format to handle collisions. A time-based global least recently used (LRU) policy manages in-memory entries. During cache refreshes, the system uses access history to preload translations accessed within the previous 15 minutes, avoiding a cold cache after the swap.

In one example, a translation dataset that previously consumed approximately 800 MB in memory required around 40 MB for metadata after the redesign. With a configured limit of 50,000 in-memory entries, actual memory consumption typically ranged between 80 MB and 120 MB. In another reported workload, approximately 30,000 of more than four million entries were loaded in memory, while the cache hit rate remained above 99.9%. The p99 latency for disk-backed cache misses stayed below 100 microseconds.

Memory usage decreased from approximately 2.7 GB to 750 MB (Source: Uber Blog Post)

Uber's experience highlights the cost implications of in-memory caching at scale. The team recommends minimizing object references to reduce GC overhead and measuring how frequently cached values are accessed. When only a small proportion of cached data is actively used, a hybrid approach can retain frequently accessed values in memory while moving the rest to disk.

#9892. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

Visual document retrieval and RAG with NeoMME-Retriever

Visual document retrieval and RAG with NeoMME-Retriever
