#9845. Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs

This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI.

The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative.

Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia.

The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance?

For these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things.

My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the important quality criteria.

I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI. However, SwiftUI has performance issues (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front.

While desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are important for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems.

Thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native. I believe 1Password has this architecture. This is also the "Phoenix" plan for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop.

That said, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust. Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view. You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks. Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit.

One of the big unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout. It is of course a hard problem to get right. I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley. It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community. It seems to be used in the majority of new Rust UI toolkits. In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative.

AccessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits. I should note, though, there is a difference between a good integration and a box ticking exercise. And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible. One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled. This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design.

One topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor. This issue is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video. You really want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates.

There has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet. To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely. Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms. On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU.

This is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks. But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not.

One of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs. The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases.

That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and update the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor.

For this reason among others, I am not impressed by the choice of the ArtCraft projects to use egui. I do think egui is a really good implementation of the immediate mode paradigm in Rust, and it does solve a number of problems (including accessibility, something mainline Iced does not yet support), but it wouldn’t be my first choice for productivity and design applications. The egui README is quite honest on the advantages and disadvantages, and is worth consulting.

One theme that’s emerging from trying to do LLM-assisted software engineering well is having clearly scoped modules, ideally with solid specifications of what the module does. Within a module, given clear objectives such as performance and robustness against adverse inputs, an LLM can do very well.

This philosophy is in tension with what has historically worked well. People reasonably choose a UI toolkit based on how good it looks. In particular, Apple UI frameworks have an immense amount of design knowledge baked in, especially in the defaults. With very little effort, it’s possible for a developer to make an app that looks and feels like a Mac app, even if not very polished.

I think in the future we should be moving toward a separation of design and execution. Both are hard problems, but very different. I’m especially excited about how much room there is to improve the execution side when really optimizing. As discussed in the 2022 blog post, the computer science core of a UI toolkit is an incremental computation engine.

Having a good spec at the interface between design and execution is critically important. As a general strategy, I suggest adapting web standards, but not following them slavishly. Web standards are an impressive and important artifact. A huge amount of time and energy has gone into producing them, and there’s also a lot of care to making things work cross-platform. The extensive WPT tests are the true magic of the spec, aiding correctness in the multiple high quality open source implementations. All this goes a long way to explaining why Electron is popular.

That said, strictly adhering to web standards has serious downsides. DOM is slow and memory-intensive; a lighter weight tree representation with a bulk mutation interface might serve the need of GUI apps better. Full CSS style resolution and layout is also expensive, though CSS is a rich and powerful way to describe styling. A subset of CSS carefully curated for efficiency might be useful. I’ve done experiments in implementing selectors as an efficient state machine that supports incremental evaluation, at the expense of fancier CSS features such as sibling selectors.

The Web is also lacking a solid way to represent virtualized lists, a core feature of every efficient UI toolkit. A spec here requires nailing down the interface with the data model, preserving incrementality.

Blitz, as a modular browser engine, is well placed to serve as the cornerstone of hybrid approaches borrowing heavily from Web specs, but also adapting them to be higher performance and more tightly integrated with platform capabilities. As just one example, it’s possible to start with Stylo as the CSS selector engine, and then replace it with a leaner, more efficient CSS engine if that proves to be practical.

One good example of separation of concerns into smaller modules is the Xilem/Masonry split. The Xilem reactive layer was designed to be independent of the actual elements it controls, and indeed it has instantiations both for DOM (which, among other things, is the infrastructure for the squircle interactive demo) and Masonry widgets. Masonry, on the other hand, was designed to be independent of the reactive layer and indeed the language for the layer above it.

By contrast, SwiftUI mashes together the low level widget implementation, the reactivity framework, and the language as well; Swift runtime reflection is part of the execution engine. Obviously SwiftUI has had a lot farther reach than Xilem, but my argument today is that we should reconsider assumptions as things are rapidly changing.

Given a UI design encoded in a certain way – which can be code, data, or a combination of the two in a DSL – an engine has a number of opportunities to optimize the execution of that design. Perhaps a lot of this section is gilding the lily, as a straightforward evaluation of the design in optimized Rust code will outperform almost any shipping GUI. But I’m interested in the limits of what performance is possible. Can we get silky smooth UI even on low end Android phones? I think the answer is yes, and the question worth exploring.

One useful tactic may be separating out the static from the dynamic parts of the design, and precomputing the static parts. That in no way precludes the design having dynamic parts; it's just that it may be possible to avoid the cost of a fully dynamic implementation.

Another fruitful avenue for optimization is optimizing the use of layers, to be composited either using the system compositor or a lightweight GPU-accelerated polyfill. Using layers effectively can dramatically improve performance, mostly by avoiding re-rendering of parts of the interface that haven't changed. However, layers have a RAM cost, and using too many layers can actually slow things down, as allocating new layers has to go through calls to the underlying system. Getting this right is a tricky optimization problem, and a good use of either measurement or analysis. UI toolkits generally either use heuristics, which are not always perfect, or explicit hints (like .drawingGroup() in SwiftUI or RepaintBoundary in Flutter).

For a deeper dive into performance questions, see A Critique of GPUI. Ideally, there aren't huge performance differences between UI toolkits, as all low hanging fruit should be picked. We expect implementations of system languages to be quite comparable in performance, but still tolerate wide discrepancies in GUI performance.

Thanks to Nico Burns for reviewing an earlier draft of this post.

#9844. AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

An organization's ability to quickly recover from a business disruption will be a competitive advantage in an era of AI-driven threats and business enablement.

Commvault SHIFT — Nashville, Tenn. — Enterprise data recovery practices must evolve from a last-resort response to a continuous operational discipline focused on minimizing business disruption and containing the blast radius of cyber incidents as quickly as possible.

That was the central message at Commvault's SHIFT 2026 conference this week, where security executives highlighted the growing importance of making operational resilience a business priority as AI-driven threats and increasingly autonomous business processes complicate the task of maintaining continuity.

"AI is changing the durable advantage you have built for your business, your brand, your supply chain, your data," said Sanjay Mirchandani, president and CEO of Commvault, in a keynote address at the event. "In the AI era, resilience will be your new competitive advantage."

Two developments are driving the trend. On the threat side, AI is giving attackers the ability to automate and accelerate reconnaissance, exploit development, social engineering, and lateral movement. The trend has compressed the time organizations have to detect and contain an intrusion, Mirchandani and other executives at the event noted.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

At the same time, enterprises are increasingly embedding AI into business processes, workflows and decision-making, creating new dependencies on data, applications and autonomous systems.

The result is a more complex operating environment in which a disruption can have wider and faster consequences, making the ability to contain incidents, preserve trusted operations and recover without derailing business activity more important than ever.

Attackers these days are able to move faster with a level of automation not available before, noted Rajeev Kottomtharayil, chief products officer at Commvault. Increasingly, recovery is becoming not just about speed but bringing back clean data. "If everything is under attack, how do we know what to trust? The real goal is to have a clean, safe space to recover even if everything around you has been compromised," Kottomtharayil said.

Business innovation and enablement are also driving the need for greater operational resilience. Resilient operations give organizations the confidence to experiment with AI and put it to work across the business, while ensuring they can recover quickly when something goes wrong, said Pragnesh Dave, head of generative AI and ML sales at AWS. "AI is collapsing the amount of time it takes to move from an idea to an outcome," he said during a keynote session. As a result, the competitive advantage will come not simply from how quickly organizations can turn intelligence into action, but from how quickly they can do so while managing the risks and consequences when those actions sometimes prove wrong.

Related:Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering

Dave pointed to the operations model at Amazon that emphasizes the notion of the "door swinging both ways" when teams try to innovate. It is an approach that has enabled teams at Amazon to code more than four times faster than before, he said.

"The question for everyone is not if something is going to break," he said. Rather, it is about what the blast radius is and the time it takes from when something breaks to recovering to the prior trusted state. "If something goes wrong, you need to be able to recover quickly. You should be able to walk back a decision. Think of your recovery time as your innovation project."

Continuous detection and continuous recovery are going to become a baseline requirement for organizations, argued Peter Diamandis, futurist, entrepreneur, and founder and chairman of the XPRIZE Foundation. Over the next few years, he foresees all organizations harnessing AI to migrate a significant workload to the "digital edge" with humans providing judgement, taste, and oversight. "AI gives us all access to capabilities that were once scarce." The qualities that matter the most will be the speed at which an organization can innovate and that requires standing up capabilities to recover quickly when failures do occur, he said during a keynote address.

Related:Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

At the same time, recovery is not becoming a substitute for prevention, says Bill O'Connell, chief security officer at Commvault. Both are equally important. But "building the highest walls and the deepest moat" to keep threats out alone is no longer enough. Organizations have to equally focus on building an ability to recover quickly to a trusted state regardless of the reason for a disruption and to thoroughly test that ability before it becomes necessary.

The key to keep in mind is that while AI has dramatically accelerated the pace of change it hasn’t altered the need for traditional, and long-familiar, IT governance and controls around their assets, identities, access, authentication and authentication, O'Connell says. "The IT maintenance and housekeeping elements still matter." When organizations have supercharged tools which they are not entirely sure how to govern, they need to make sure those fundamentals remain in place.

In enabling better resilience, organizations should also evaluate what impact third parties could have on their ability to quickly restore operations, O'Connell says. For years, organizations have used questionnaires and external vendor risk-scoring services to try and assess third-party risk. In the AI era, security teams need to go a step further with their most critical suppliers, he adds. O'Connell suggested organizations have their technical architects work with their counterparts at third-party suppliers to understand how critical services are actually configured and what would happen if a provider experienced a breach or a disruption.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9843. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

#9841. My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%

Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!

My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.

I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.

But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦

Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.

I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.

So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.

The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.

Then I tried flow control. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast…

I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.

Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the issue is not the monitor again? But it has to be!

Well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:

So basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.

Why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!

When the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.

Here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an issue. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.

As you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.

Well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this.

I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask.

The problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the issues don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1…

So I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a new adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead: UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter. My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did!

Why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself:

I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac.

I think the big takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets?

See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from!

#9839. Attackers Say 'Hello' to a Different Scale of Cloud Attack

Researchers dubbed an attack chain "Greeter" after discovering that attackers deliberately covered their trail by leaving "hello" messages in logs.

What began as an exploratory Shodan search for exposed cloud instances has led to the discovery of a broad-ranging AI infrastructure attack campaign that researchers have christened "Greeter." The campaign, which started life as an organized, multistage, systematic attack across cloud providers, reinforces why defenders need to shift their thinking about cloud security to include a layered model built around network access control, data protection, and identity security.

Era Security researchers kicked off the research when the Shodan search engine revealed open Amazon DynamoDB instances where anyone could download data or delete it entirely. They dug a little deeper and found Flowise, a connected open source GenAI development platform, where users can build AI agents powered by large language models (LLMs).

Roughly 90% of the nearly 3,000 scanned Flowise deployments were running unpatched versions vulnerable to a critical code-injection vulnerability, CVE-2024-58351 — and if the researchers could see it, so could attackers. So, Era Security deployed AI-powered honeypots, mostly on Amazon Web Service (AWS), to catch them in action.

Related:LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

Honeypot technology is "not like it was before," and attackers don't recognize it's a decoy until they're much further into the environment, according to the Era Security research team. In the past, it took three or fourth months to build a realistic honeypot. Today, it's two hours.

"The most important finding wasn't the exploitation technique itself, but it was what happened after," Naor Talmor, chief technology officer (CTO) at Era Security, tells Dark Reading. What ensued was a repeatable, staged methodology where attackers mapped out privileges and the environment, hunted for credentials, exploited cloud metadata services across multiple providers to escalate access, and then locked in persistence, he explains. Attackers also obfuscated their activity by leaving seemingly benign and fleeting "hello" messages in the logs, making detection much more difficult because it requires team to spend time searching for specific indicators of compromise in the logs. Thus, the researchers gave the campaign the "Greeter" moniker.

The sophisticated techniques and persistence show that Greeter isn't an opportunistic smash-and-grab attack, a script kiddie, or someone who had merely stumbled upon the honeypots, the researchers noted. And, the campaign was deployed across several AWS regions at once, which indicates broader scale and intent.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Era Security warns of the potential scale the campaign could reach, confirming 46 real-world victims so far, based on the number of unauthenticated instances that mirrored the honeypot conditions. The team estimates that at least 50% of those remain connected to the Internet and visible, suggesting at least 20 organizations are currently exposed. The sophistication levels of the the threat actors also speaks to how how valuable the cloud and AI attack surface has become, given the effort required to launch Greeter; this wasn't low-hanging fruit.

The Greeter campaign signals a few shifts across the cloud landscape, including how much easier it's gotten for attackers to go unnoticed in workflows. Much of that is due to AI, which threat actors are using to assist in writing code or orchestrating attack steps, according to the Greeter attack logs.

A decade ago, cloud attacks targeted the Docker API. Threat actors then began exploiting workloads, escaping containers to reach the cloud's metadata server underneath, and exploiting service accounts from there, the researchers explain. While attackers are following a similar pattern, they are now using AI infrastructure as the new way to establish persistence.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

Researchers agree that the end goal on each instance was to grab cloud credentials and perform lateral movement within a targeted organization.

Meanwhile, attribution remains quite challenging. When the researchers drilled down to the code and techniques, they started to see Chinese characters, though that could be a false flag. Still, a nation-state culprit would make since, because the notion of seeing an "entire orchestration, not even a big cybercrime group could execute that," according to Era Security.

The current velocity of vulnerability exploitation is nothing like the researchers have seen in the past, which puts immense pressure on organizations' traditional patching cycles. This played out just over the past few weeks alone, as security teams raced to fix PHP2Shell and OpenSSH, searching workloads one by one for flaws. However, the Greeter campaign shows a defense challenge for cloud security that's bigger than fixing any specific vulnerability.

Everyone needs to assume a breach now, warns Talmor, adding how if it's not a vulnerability, it may be leaked credentials or an exposed API. Organizations need to design security programs around the cloud to be ready for all of the above, he advises, adopting defense-in-depth.

"A lot of companies adopt that, but they don't really practice it," he notes.

The researchers say organizations can detect this kind of attack much faster if teams monitor for enumeration activity to close gaps before attackers find them. When applications or chat tools are installed, logging can be activated and streamed to a separate location so that even if attackers do delete a device's local history, the logs remain stored in the cloud.

Researchers also noted that this should be monitored closely in critical environments, especially where crown jewels or critical applications are involved, adding that organizations can have dozens or hundreds of accounts depending on the size.

"To be clear, we aren't saying, 'Stop caring about misconfigurations or stop caring about vulnerabilities," Talmor says, warning that patch management is a game "we are losing" that requires organizations to secure their environment layer by layer.

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Lambda Now Runs GPU Inference with 48 Concurrent Invocations Sharing One Model per GPU

Nov 22, 2026 4 min read

AWS has added GPU support to AWS Lambda: Event Functions running on Lambda Managed Instances can now run on EC2 G-series instances (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f and G6e at launch), deployed as container images, and triggered by the same event sources as any other function. The feature is generally available in the commercial regions where both Managed Instances and G-series instances exist. It is priced at the EC2 On-Demand rate plus a 9.75 percent management fee and the standard $0.20 per million requests.

As InfoQ reported last December, Managed Instances let a function run on EC2 capacity the customer selects and pays for, with Lambda handling provisioning, patching and scaling and several invocations sharing one execution environment. GPUs were missing at that launch. Daniel Abib, senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, describes the operator's side of the change:

You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate.

A capacity provider lists the allowed instance types, the VPC and a vCPU ceiling; Lambda picks the newest generation with capacity and falls back to older generations when newer ones are short:

The function declares its GPU memory through a new AcceleratorConfig block, next to memory, timeout, storage, and a per-environment concurrency:

Concurrent invocations in one environment share a single copy of the model in GPU memory, up to 48 per environment, and scaling follows GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and concurrency. Publishing a version provisions the environments, downloads the weights, and warms the engine before the first event arrives; Seekable OCI lazy loading can cut environment start time by up to 70 percent.

AWS ships five GPU base images: CUDA only, CuPy, PyTorch, vLLM, and SGLang. The two inference servers need no handler code; a MODEL_ID variable points to a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an S3 prefix, or a local path, and a model swap is a configuration change followed by a new version:

The limits are in the launch post: container images up to 32 GB, 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2 to 32 GB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider, and a timeout of up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations. Abib draws the line against the competition in one sentence: serverless GPU services that hide the same work "often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking."

The first hands-on reports came within a day. Classmethod's Akaike, who had corrected a conference talk in December after finding that no G-type was accepted, tried every accelerated instance type in us-east-1 and found 37 of 81 accepted, all G-family; P-family, G7, Inferentia, Trainium, and the Graviton-based g5g were refused, as were zip packages. A PyTorch benchmark ran about 66 times faster on the L4 than on the instance's CPU. Still, neither Terraform nor the Cloud Control provider knew AcceleratorConfig yet, and the GPU vCPU quota in a fresh account is zero: "if you use g6.xlarge (4 vCPU) with the default three instances, you need a quota of 12 vCPUs." A Terraform provider issue and pull request, opened on 16 November by a user named sasidhar-aws, and a pull request from the same user remain open.

A second test, by an AWS Community Builder writing as xbill, put Gemma 4 E2B on a single g6.2xlarge through the vLLM image, with Google's 4-bit QAT weights and a speculative-decoding drafter baked into a 9 GB image. One environment served all 48 simultaneous requests and every one of 417 calls succeeded, at roughly 130 tokens a second for a single request and 3,400 to 3,600 at 48. The friction was in the pipeline rather than the GPU: 484 seconds from publish to an active version, a Docker image index that Lambda rejected until it was pushed as a single-platform manifest, and a handler that returns complete replies, so time to first token could not be measured. His verdict keeps to that scope:

For a model behind events, queues or other AWS services, the Lambda GPU function is the simpler road: one image, one function, and Lambda keeps the server alive and routes the requests. Keep the drafter on for a chat with a few users at a time, and publish without it for heavy batch load.

When streamed replies or full control of the server are needed, he writes, "run vLLM on an EC2 G6 yourself."

The pricing model is the one Managed Instances introduced, with a lower fee for GPUs than the 15 percent charged on CPU instance types. Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply to the instance, and there is no duration charge, so an instance bills for as long as the minimum environment count is above zero. Yan Cui's December analysis of the model, written when it still carried the line "GPU instances are NOT supported," applies to the GPU case unchanged:

Regular Lambda functions can scale rapidly by tapping into a large, shared pool of EC2 instances. With managed instances, it takes tens of seconds to launch new EC2 instances. As such, it's not a good fit when you have large, unpredictable spikes in traffic.

Managed Instances still support only Event Functions, so the GPU path does not yet reach Web Functions, the HTTP-server shape Lambda gained this year, and AWS has not said whether it will.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#9837. Testing Terraform with AWS Emulator

Terraform plan passes and shows all green and all the necessary resource changes. You trigger apply and... the job fails with some obscure error that a resource can't be changed. You open another pull request and try again. And perhaps you encounter an error again. Sounds familiar? I bet it does. I encountered issues like this so many times I'm afraid to count. But recently AWS released a new tool called Emulator that emulates actual AWS API endpoints. And it should be great for tasks just like that!

The problem with the difference between plan and apply jobs is that plan can't possibly emulate every actual API call against a live infrastructure. It's a safe assumption based on the static declarations we put into it – the order of application, the necessary parameters, the proper configuration values. These mock calls can't know for a fact that you already have a resource in AWS called "my-bucket-asdasdasd" or that you're trying to upgrade a PostgreSQL RDS instance from version 14 to version 18 without an explicit "apply immediately" flag. One may argue that one can always try to apply changes locally, but this kinda undermines the whole automation workflow. So what is the answer?

There are multiple tools that can emulate AWS services either partially or in full, but what they lack is the actual knowledge of the service architecture. It may be similar, but it won't be authentic, and sometimes this small difference may cause a lot of problems. After all, what can be the closest to an AWS API, if not the same AWS API, but ephemeral?

The benefit of the AWS Emulator is that it's a self-contained binary (or Docker container) that can be utilized locally or in a CI workflow. This means the usual "Plan > Apply" terraform workflow changes to "Plan > Apply against mock AWS infrastructure to test the plan > Apply on actual AWS Infrastructure". This means slightly longer jobs, but if you're like me and apply jobs run on commits to the main branch after a PR, this saves you the hassle of creating a new branch just to fix the issue.

Let's start with a local setup and see how we can utilize AWS Emulator with the actual Terraform code. All code is available in my example GitHub repository.

First up, installation. You can either install aws-emulator via package manager, or build it with Docker. I'll use Docker to keep my system clear of yet another package:

And it's up and running! In the example above I set the container to live without limits (official AWS documentation proposes to set memory and swap limits: --memory=2g --memory-swap=2g, but for local that's fine). I also disabled authorization (flag -a off) to simplify things a bit.

To be sure aws-emulator is up and running, let's query the admin endpoint:

Okay, fake AWS is live, let's deploy some infrastructure!

I created an example AWS stack for Terraform and will use it in this article. First, let's configure Terraform to act against aws-emulator and not real AWS APIs. providers.tf will look like this:

The difference between actual live infrastructure and a fake one is that we set up a bunch of flags to allow insecure connections (perhaps turning authentication off wasn't actually simpler?) and we set up an endpoint for each service we use in the setup to an emulator endpoint, which lives in the local Docker container:

The rest of the configuration is as usual: resources, variables, modules (if any). Just what your project has.

Let's proceed and test our setup. (I'll omit full terraform output otherwise this article would be 3 kilometers long)

Plan works! That's good to see, but not what we're here for. Still, a good sign. Now for the real test.

Sadly, the running aws-emulator container doesn't show in its logs which API requests it receives and what's happening under the hood, but I guess the tool is good enough as it is.

A container started with --rm removes itself after stopping, so no additional cleanup is needed. And as for the emulator -- it stores its state in memory, so each container restart drops all record of previous actions and any stale state.

Now for the real test: can we wrap the desired logic inside a CI pipeline? Let's think.

For successful invocation in the pipeline we will need almost everything the same, but we will be limited by time (the faster -- the better, and overall reasonable timeouts) and resources.

The workflow with terraform apply against aws-emulator is shown down below. For it I decided to try out package manager installation (builders are ephemeral anyway) and proper authentication. Full workflow with actual successful runs can be found in the example GitHub repository.

This is a crude excerpt of the actual glorious workflow file that outlines the most important steps: emulator installation, terraform setup, plan and apply. On the example terraform architecture the whole pipeline took 1m25s, which is okay in my opinion, but there is room for improvement: sprinkle some caching on top, leave validation, format check for local hooks, etc.

It's always nice when code someone wrote on the internet works from the start after you copy-paste it onto your machine. That's why I always run the described processes myself -- building, testing, fixing, retrying -- before publishing an article. But showing only the positive scenarios creates a false sense of trust in the tool.

In the example codebase I added a variable that, when enabled, makes the stack try to deploy a resource with an erroneous declaration. It will pass the plan job, but fail on apply.

Setting this variable to true at runtime will break our stack. Let's see:

And there we have it. The exact issue that arises only against actual API calls and not during a plan job.

For scenarios exactly like this, the emulator is priceless.

AWS Emulator is AWESOME. I'm rarely that excited about new tools lately (mostly because almost all of them are near/about AI), but this one is just so good and scratches that exact itch I felt for so long.

For starters, it can't effectively emulate IAM policies and permission checks. This is a bummer, because permission validation is such a crucial step for production-ready security. Here's hoping that the tool will evolve further and it will be included in future updates.

Second, as a tool still a work-in-progress[1], its capabilities are quite limited. Even while writing the article I encountered several cases of 501 NotImplemented. It complicates things a bit if your infrastructure setup is huge and has a lot of quirks and weird configurations and super new services. Still, AWS releases new versions quite often, and they're quite open about Emulator limitations, which is nice.

And last, but not least, is telemetry. AWS is explicit that it gathers telemetry and what this telemetry includes. This is honest behaviour and I like that approach. They even allow you to disable the telemetry, which further increases my trust in this tool. I understand the rationale behind this functionality (the tool is actively developed, they need the data to understand usage patterns and what goes wrong), but in the age of constant surveillance from Big Tech at every corner it still raises a slight concern. But then again, for the ultra-paranoid folks the code is open source and can be rebuilt with telemetry torn out of it.

As of the moment of writing this article, AWS Emulator has been live for 1 day. ↩︎

#9836. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

日本においてサイバー攻撃や情報漏洩が急増していることを受け、日本政府は、攻撃に迅速に対応し、インフラのセキュリティを強化するための産官の専門家チームを設立することを目的とした、100億円（6,300万ドル）規模の緊急サイバーセキュリティ対策パッケージを可決した。

この戦略の4つの柱には、サイバー防衛へのAI導入を含む基礎的なサイバーセキュリティ対策の全国的な徹底、国内のサイバー捜査能力の強化、サイバー攻撃の被害者への支援拡充、そして民間企業と連携してサイバー攻撃に共同で対応することが含まれている。

高市早苗首相は、国のサイバーレジリエンス（回復力）を高めるため、これらのサイバーセキュリティ対策を「迅速かつ効果的に」実施するよう求めた。

「今この瞬間も、不正アクセスや情報漏洩の事案が後を絶たず、人々の日常生活や企業活動に多大な影響を及ぼしている」と、高市早苗首相は11月6日に緊急対策パッケージを発表した際の声明で述べた。「政府のあらゆる資源を動員し、サイバー攻撃への対応能力を全面的に強化していこう。」

サイバー攻撃の急増は、日本企業や政府機関に甚大な被害をもたらしている。サイバーセキュリティ企業（旧トレンドマイクロ）であるTrendAIのデータによると、2026年の最初の9か月間で600件以上のサイバーセキュリティインシデントが公表され、2025年通年の594件を上回った。公表されている報告数は控えめな推計に過ぎない。日本の個人情報保護監督機関は、4月から10月中旬にかけて2,094件の情報漏洩事案を記録しており（原文は日本語）、これも2025年度通年の総件数を上回っている。

他の地域ではAIが攻撃者を支援しているものの、サイバーセキュリティ企業TrendAIの脅威調査共同責任者であるライアン・フローレス氏は、脅威に関する声明の中で、インシデントの増加と攻撃者によるAIの利用との間に明確な関連性は確認されていないと述べた。

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

「サイバー攻撃は世界的に増加しており、その結果として侵害やデータ漏洩も増加しています」と同氏は述べた。「AIが直接関与しているわけではないかもしれませんが、攻撃者が標的を見つけたり、操作を自動化したりするのを支援するAIの能力により、サイバー攻撃は大規模化しています。組織は、被害に遭う確率を下げるために、サイバーリスクを低減し、脆弱性を解消する必要があります。」

最近の侵害事例には、冷凍食品大手のニチレイやビール・食品大手のアサヒに対するランサムウェア攻撃、およびGMOインターネットグループを標的としたデータ侵害などが含まれる。これらの攻撃の多くは犯罪的な性質を持つが、盗まれた情報が他の犯罪グループや国家主体のアクターによって、日本の国民に対して悪用される可能性があることが懸念されていると、日本の通信大手NTTのチーフ・サイバーセキュリティ・ストラテジスト、松原美穂子氏は指摘する。

「攻撃者が十分な個人情報を収集・集約できれば、個人の嗜好から経済活動に至るまで、日本国民の詳細なプロファイルを構築できる」と同氏は述べる。「そのデータは、世論を操作したり、日本の機関に対する信頼を損なわせたりするための標的型偽情報キャンペーンなど、日本に対する影響工作に利用される可能性がある」

日本政府は、緊急資金を活用して、サイバーセキュリティ体制全体を強化するための4つの広範な取り組みを推進する意向だ。閣僚会議の公表された議事録によると、政府は、最近の多くの情報漏洩は適切なセキュリティ対策によって防ぐことができたはずだと指摘し、最初の取り組みとして、各組織が基本的なサイバーセキュリティ対策を確実に実施するよう促すとしている。

2つ目の主要な取り組みは、調査および情報収集能力を向上させ、より精度の高い分析を可能にし、その結果を国民に提供することで、攻撃への備えを強化することである。第三に、政府はサイバー攻撃への対応を強化し、国際的なパートナーシップを構築するとともに、積極的なサイバー防衛措置を実施する。最後に、政府は被害者を支援する能力とインフラを整備し、市民が損害を回復し、企業が事業を継続できるようにする計画だ。

「被害を受けた組織や個人が迷うことなく支援を受けられるよう、利用しやすい相談窓口や専門家による直接的な支援を拡充し、二次被害を防ぐための情報共有を強化する」と、日本の議事録には記されている。「また、官民の専門家を柔軟に派遣するための全国的な仕組みの構築にも着手する」

10月1日、日本の「積極的サイバー防衛法」が施行され、警察や自衛隊（SDF）に対し、日本の国家安全保障にリスクをもたらすあらゆるサイバー攻撃に対して強力な措置を講じる権限が与えられた。

「多くの国が、日本がいかなる種類のサイバー攻撃に対して、どれほどの速さで、どの程度の強度で対応できるのかを知りたがっているだろう」とNTTの松原氏は述べ、次のように付け加えた。「この緊急対策パッケージは……法律の枠組みを経済全体にわたる実用的な能力へと転換し、攻撃の可能性が高まる中、あらゆる規模の組織が攻撃を予防、検知、対応できるよう準備するために必要である。」

しかし、この資金はあくまで第一歩に過ぎず、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの投資を継続するには、さらなる資金が必要になると同氏は指摘する。

「この対策パッケージの重要な点は、サイバーセキュリティを個々の組織に完全に任せておくことはできないという認識が示されていることだ」と松原氏は述べる。「セキュリティ評価やインシデント対応、復旧支援といった形の政府による支援が、大きな違いを生むことができる。」

#9831. Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The package adds public-private cyber responders, an AI-focused team run by the economic ministry, and more leeway to use the government's new active cyber-defense powers.

To read this story in Japanese, please click here (translation by our internal AI tool).

With Japan facing a surge in cyberattacks and breaches, the Japanese government has passed a ¥10 billion ($63 million) emergency cybersecurity package aimed at establishing teams of industry and government experts to quickly respond to attacks and better secure its infrastructure.

The four pillars of the strategy include thoroughly implementing basic cybersecurity measures country-wide, including adopting AI for cyber-defense, strengthening the nation's cyber-investigations capabilities, better supporting the victims of cyberattacks, and partnering with private industry to jointly respond to cyberattacks.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called for the cybersecurity measures to be implemented "promptly and effectively" to enhance the nation's cyber resilience.

"Even at this very moment, incidents of unauthorized access and information leaks continue to occur, significantly affecting people's daily lives and business activities," Takaichi said in a published statement announcing the emergency package on November 6. "Let us mobilize the full resources of the Government to strengthen Japan's overall capabilities to respond to cyberattacks."

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

While AI has aided attackers elsewhere, TrendAI has not established a firm link between the increases and the use of AI by attackers, Ryan Flores, co-lead for threat research at TrendAI, a cybersecurity firm, said in a statement on the threats.

"Cyberattacks are increasing globally, and so are the breaches and data leaks as a result," he said. "While AI might not be directly involved, its ability to help the attackers find targets and automate their operations makes cyberattacks scalable. Organizations need to shrink their cyber exposure and close the vulnerabilities in order to lower the odds of being victimized."

Recent compromises include ransomware attacks on business, such as frozen food giant Nichirei and brewery and food giant Asahi, and data breaches targeting GMO Internet Group. While many of the attacks are criminal in nature, the worry is that the stolen information could be used by other criminal groups and nation-state actors against the Japanese public, says Mihoko Matsubara, chief cybersecurity strategist for Japanese telecom giant NTT.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

"If attackers can collect and aggregate enough personal information, they can build detailed profiles of Japanese citizens, from personal preferences to economic activities," she says. "That data could potentially be used for influence operations against Japan, such as targeted disinformation campaigns to manipulate public opinion or undermine trust in Japanese institutions."

The Japanese government intends to use the emergency funding to pursue four broad initiatives to improve its overall cybersecurity posture. Pointing out that many recent breaches could have been prevented by good hygiene, the government's first initiative is to ensure organizations are implementing basic cybersecurity measures, according to the published Japanese notes of the ministerial meeting.

The second major initiative is to improve investigation and information collection capabilities, allowing better analysis that can then be delivered to the public to better prepare them for attacks. Third, the government will strengthen its response to cyberattacks, establishing international partnerships and implementing active cyber-defense measures. Finally, the government plans to create the capability and infrastructure to support victims so that citizens can recover damages and businesses can remain operational.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

"Accessible consultation points and direct expert support will be expanded so that affected organizations and individuals can connect to support without confusion, and communication to prevent secondary harm will be strengthened," the Japanese notes stated. "Work will also begin on building a nationwide mechanism for flexibly dispatching public- and private-sector specialists."

On October 1, Japan's Active Cyber Defense legislation came into effect, authorizing the police and the Self-Defense Forces (SDF) to take strong measures against any cyberattacks that pose a risk to Japan’s national security.

"Many countries would be keen to learn how quickly Japan could respond to which kind of cyberattacks, and with what level of intensity," says NTT's Matsubara, adding: "This emergency package is ... necessary to translate the law’s framework into practical capabilities across the broader economy, preparing organizations of all sizes to prevent, detect and respond to attacks as they become increasingly likely."

However, the funds are only enough to get started, and more will be necessary to continue Japan's investment in cybersecurity, she says.

"The important aspect about this package is that it recognizes that cybersecurity cannot be left entirely to individual organizations," Matsubara says. "Government assistance, in the form of security assessments and incident response or recovery support, can make a difference."

#9830. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

#9828. [$] Added indirection allows for larger BPF programs

The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.
